overview: Late medieval Zapotec Oaxaca contained competing kingdoms and towns, including Mitla and Yagul. The map label “Zapotec Empire” should not imply that one ruler governed this entire outline. These communities inherited a much longer history of cities, trade and writing.

periods.title: Earlier urban foundations
periods.summary: Classic-period communities such as Lambityeco combined household production with larger political networks.

periods.title: Several regional centres
periods.summary: Mitla rose after Monte Albán’s decline; later kingdoms developed distinctive palaces and ceremonial places.

periods.title: Conquest and reorganization
periods.summary: Spanish campaigns, local alliances and colonial resettlement changed the political landscape.

sections.title: Palaces and a city under the trees

items.text: Yagul’s Palace of Six Patios included spaces interpreted as public and private, with central courts perhaps used by the ruler’s family. Doorways and room arrangements help archaeologists investigate who could enter and how household life overlapped with government.

Mitla’s great columned hall used six large stone columns to support wooden beams and a flat roof. INAH suggests a civic or administrative function. Those columns were practical engineering as well as an impressive sight for anyone entering the room.

The famous geometric patterns at Mitla were made in several ways. Some use many small fitted stones; others carve larger sections into single blocks. From a distance they can resemble patterned cloth, but a close view reveals the stoneworker’s planning and precision.

A 2025 lidar study mapped more than 1,100 buildings at Guiengola, a fifteenth-century Zapotec settlement. Laser measurements revealed a fortified city covering about 360 hectares, with roads, temples and ballcourts, rather than simply a soldiers’ fortress.

Guiengola had different neighbourhoods for elites and commoners. Comparing the space occupied by residences and ceremonial buildings gives researchers a way to investigate inequality. The families who cooked, repaired houses and supplied the city belonged in its history too.

Earlier evidence from Lambityeco connects salt production directly with ordinary houses. At least nine of twenty-three production mounds examined in a research study also had evidence of commoner residences. Work could happen around the home rather than in one central factory.

Those salt-working areas were scattered around Lambityeco. Their distribution suggests that producers were not all confined to a single workshop or neighbourhood. This is Classic-period background, several centuries earlier than the map’s 1279 starting snapshot.

In a much later example, Zapotec textile artist Porfirio Gutiérrez works with natural dyes and knowledge learned through family practice. Cactus-dwelling cochineal insects produce a powerful red dye. A colour farm can be small enough to grow on cactus pads.

Gutiérrez’s work links Teotitlán del Valle with a Zapotec community in California. His studio offers younger people a way to learn weaving, dyeing and care for plants. This is a modern continuation of knowledge, not a claim that every medieval loom worked identically.

A tiny colonial Zapotec sample is “Niça”, meaning “water”. Juan de Córdova printed it on folio 9r of his 1578 grammar. The Ticha project preserves the wording: this is Latin-script Zapotec recorded after conquest, distinct from the region’s earlier hieroglyphic traditions.

Ticha also preserves seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Zapotec wills and legal documents. These texts let readers encounter people arranging property and family affairs in their own language. They extend the written record beyond royal monuments and famous battles.

Spanish authorities relocated Yagul’s population during the sixteenth century to help form Santa María de la Asunción Tlacolula. Moving a town changed where people lived; it did not mean that Zapotec communities or languages ceased to exist.

ending.text: Spanish conquest and colonial administration reshaped different Zapotec kingdoms during the sixteenth century, through campaigns, alliances and resettlement. There was no single empire ending at the map’s 1492 cutoff. Zapotec communities continue in Oaxaca and beyond.
